strengths: Novel perspective on token-level visual dependency with clear empirical validation showing sparse distribution of visually-grounded tokens
Comprehensive experimental evaluation on 8 diverse benchmarks with consistent improvements (19.2% for 7B, 7.6% for 32B) across strong baselines
Thorough ablation studies validating both components (TAS and TGF) and demonstrating sensitivity analysis for key hyperparameters
Improved training dynamics with faster convergence and better stability compared to DAPO and GRPO baselines
Strong reproducibility with detailed algorithm description, hyperparameter specifications, and extensive implementation details
Effective qualitative analysis demonstrating that high-dependency tokens capture semantically meaningful concepts (geometric terms, logical connectors)
Theoretical analysis providing formal justification through variance reduction proof, though with standard assumptions
weaknesses: Limited generalization scope: only evaluated on reasoning-intensive tasks with verifiable rewards; applicability to subjective/creative tasks and very large models (72B+) unclear

Methodological choices lack principled justification: image perturbation strategy (14×14 patches at 50% drop probability), gradient filtering ratio k=0.4, and advantage scaling range [0.9, dynamic] appear empirically tuned to specific dataset

Baseline comparison concerns: DAPO requires entropy penalty (λ=0.06) to avoid policy collapse; while VPPO is more robust, the comparison is not entirely clean regarding which improvements come from better algorithm vs. better regularization robustness
Visual dependency metric design assumes random patch blackening is 'non-informative', which may not hold for images with distributed information or global context dependencies

Theoretical analysis (Theorem 3.1) relies on strong assumptions (especially Assumption 3 on dependency-advantage independence) that likely don't hold in practice; proof essentially shows filtering reduces variance, which is expected
Limited conceptual novelty of individual components; primary contribution is applying KL-divergence-based visual dependency to existing RL frameworks rather than fundamental algorithmic innovation
10% computational overhead from second forward pass with masked images is non-trivial and could limit adoption; only brief mention of future single-pass approximations
Incomplete analysis of when method works: no investigation of performance on tasks where visual dependency is not sparse, or where visual information is non-critical
Modest improvement margin over DAPO baseline (2.5% for 7B) suggests incremental rather than transformative gains despite consistent validation

strengths: Clear problem identification: Effectively identifies and motivates the uniform learning signal problem in existing multimodal RLVR methods
Comprehensive experimental validation: Evaluation on 8 diverse benchmarks with consistent 2.5% average improvement on 7B models across all tasks
Thorough ablation studies: Extensive ablations (Tables 2-7, Appendices F-I) properly validate each component and design choice
Novel perspective on token perception: Principled use of KL divergence to measure visual dependency is well-motivated and outperforms simpler heuristics
Strong execution and presentation: Well-written paper with clear figures, detailed pseudocode, and excellent organization of comprehensive appendices
Practical and generalizable method: Successfully integrated into multiple base algorithms (GRPO and DAPO) with consistent gains
Out-of-domain validation: VQA experiments confirm the method doesn't harm general visual-language capabilities and improves generalization
weaknesses: Diminishing returns at scale: 32B model shows only 1.1% average improvement compared to 7B's 2.5%, with some benchmarks below 1%, raising concerns about scalability to larger models
Computational overhead: 10% training time overhead is non-trivial and not fully justified by the modest improvements, especially on 32B models
Narrow scope and limited generalization: Only evaluated on reasoning tasks with verifiable rewards; applicability to subjective/creative tasks unclear; tested exclusively on Qwen2.5-VL

Methodological brittleness: Both baseline and VPPO require entropy penalty to prevent policy collapse (Appendix E), suggesting experimental setup instability and uncertainty about whether VPPO improvements are fundamental
Missing statistical analysis: No confidence intervals, significance tests, or error bars reported; 1-2% improvements on larger models may not be statistically significant
Weak theoretical guarantees: Variance reduction proof uses strong assumptions (uncorrelated gradients, advantage independence) with approximate bounds; lacks convergence guarantees
Limited failure analysis: Only successful qualitative examples provided; no analysis of failure modes or problem types where VPPO underperforms
Hyperparameter dependency: Design choices (k=0.4, masking strategy, entropy penalty coefficient) tuned on ViRL39K; transferability to new datasets/domains unclear
